pharm: Long-acting pegylated recombinant erythropoietin (methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta) that activates the erythropoietin receptor to stimulate red blood cell production, marketed as Mircera; allows extended (every 2-4 weeks/monthly) dosing.
tags: BOXED WARNING - thrombosis, mortality & tumor progression
quick: CKD anemia: ESA-naive 0.6 micrograms/kg IV/SC every 2 weeks (or convert from epoetin/darbepoetin to monthly dosing); titrate to hemoglobin
Intravenous or subcutaneous injection; not related to meals
Limited data; use only if clearly needed (multidose vials with benzyl alcohol avoided in pregnancy)
Endogenous erythropoietin is present in milk; limited data - caution
Used FOR anemia of chronic kidney disease; titrate to lowest dose maintaining hemoglobin
Hemoglobin (avoid >11 g/dL / rapid rise), blood pressure, iron status, thrombosis signs
summary: Methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta (a pegylated recombinant human erythropoietin marketed as Mircera) is a long-acting erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) used to treat anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adults on dialysis and not on dialysis, and in pediatric patients (per labeling). Its pegylation gives a long half-life and a different receptor interaction (continuous erythropoietin receptor activation), allowing extended dosing intervals - every 2 weeks initially and once monthly for maintenance. It stimulates erythropoiesis by the same mechanism as endogenous erythropoietin. Like all ESAs, it carries a BOXED WARNING: ESAs increase the risk of death, serious cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke), venous thromboembolism, and thrombosis of vascular access, and in cancer patients can shorten overall survival and/or hasten tumor progression. To reduce these risks, use the lowest dose needed to avoid red blood cell transfusion, do not target hemoglobin above 11 g/dL in CKD, and avoid rapid rises in hemoglobin. Mircera is NOT indicated for chemotherapy-induced anemia in cancer patients. Ensure adequate iron stores and control blood pressure during therapy.
indications: Treatment of anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adult patients on dialysis and not on dialysis
Treatment of anemia associated with CKD in pediatric patients 5-17 years on hemodialysis who are converting from another ESA after hemoglobin is stabilized (per labeling)

dosage.d: Starting dose 0.6 micrograms/kg body weight once every 2 weeks; titrate to maintain hemoglobin not exceeding 11 g/dL
dosage.n: Once hemoglobin stable, may convert to once-monthly dosing (twice the every-2-week dose)

dosage.d: Monthly dose based on prior weekly epoetin (or darbepoetin) dose per the conversion table
dosage.n: Convert when patient is on stable ESA therapy

dosage.d: Increase no more frequently than once monthly; reduce or interrupt for hemoglobin >11 g/dL or rapid rise (>1 g/dL in 2 weeks)
dosage.n: Use lowest dose sufficient to avoid red blood cell transfusion

admin: Administer by intravenous (preferred in hemodialysis) or subcutaneous injection; single-use prefilled syringes
Do not dilute or transfer between syringes; do not shake (may inactivate the glycoprotein)
Evaluate and maintain adequate iron stores (transferrin saturation and ferritin) before and during therapy
Control blood pressure adequately before starting and monitor during therapy
Store refrigerated and protect from light; provide the patient medication guide
moa: Methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta is a continuous erythropoietin receptor activator. Like endogenous erythropoietin, it stimulates erythropoiesis by interacting with the erythropoietin receptor on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, promoting their proliferation, differentiation, and survival and thereby increasing red blood cell production and hemoglobin. The integrated polyethylene glycol chain alters the molecule's interaction with the receptor (different association/dissociation kinetics) and markedly prolongs its half-life compared with epoetin, supporting extended dosing intervals while producing a sustained erythropoietic response.

absolute: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) that begins after treatment with this or other erythropoietin protein drugs
Serious allergic reactions to methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta
Use for treatment of anemia in cancer patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy (not indicated; ESAs hasten tumor progression / shorten survival)
relative: History of stroke, thromboembolism, or cardiovascular disease
Recent or planned surgery (perioperative thromboprophylaxis considerations)
monitor: Hemoglobin (avoid exceeding 11 g/dL and avoid rapid rises)
Thrombotic/cardiovascular events and signs of pure red cell aplasia (sudden loss of response)

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy. It should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; avoid multidose presentations containing benzyl alcohol. Untreated severe anemia itself poses maternal-fetal risk, so therapy may be appropriate under specialist care.
lact: Endogenous erythropoietin is present in human milk, and exogenous erythropoietin proteins are large molecules likely degraded in the infant's gastrointestinal tract with minimal absorption. Data are limited; use with caution and consider the benefits of breastfeeding alongside maternal need.
renal: This drug is specifically used to treat the anemia of chronic kidney disease. No special renal dose adjustment beyond the standard CKD titration is required; titrate to the lowest dose that maintains hemoglobin and avoids transfusion, and individualize for dialysis status.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for hepatic impairment is provided in the labeling. Use the standard hemoglobin-guided titration.

major: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions established for the ESA itself
moderate: Iron deficiency or concomitant conditions impairing erythropoiesis blunt the response - ensure adequate iron and correct other deficiencies
minor: Drugs that raise blood pressure may compound hypertension seen with ESAs
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor hemoglobin, iron indices (ferritin, transferrin saturation), and blood pressure; investigate loss of response (anti-erythropoietin antibody-mediated pure red cell aplasia).

serious: Thrombotic events - myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, vascular access thrombosis
Severe/uncontrolled hypertension and hypertensive encephalopathy / seizures
Increased mortality and accelerated tumor progression in cancer patients
Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) due to neutralizing anti-erythropoietin antibodies
rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis) reported with ESAs
emergency: Myocardial infarction, stroke, or major thrombosis

monitoring: Hemoglobin at least monthly (more often during initiation/dose changes); do not exceed 11 g/dL and avoid a rise greater than 1 g/dL in any 2-week period
Blood pressure before and during therapy; control hypertension
Iron status (ferritin and transferrin saturation) before and during therapy; supplement iron as needed
Signs of thrombosis and cardiovascular events
Investigate sudden loss of response for pure red cell aplasia (anti-erythropoietin antibodies)
counsel: This medicine helps your body make red blood cells to treat anemia from kidney disease; you will have regular blood tests to keep your hemoglobin in the target range
Tell your doctor about chest pain, leg swelling or pain, sudden weakness or trouble speaking, severe headache, or shortness of breath - these can signal a clot
Your blood pressure will be checked often; take your blood pressure medicines as prescribed and report very high readings
Adequate iron is needed for this medicine to work - take iron supplements if prescribed
Do not shake the syringe; learn proper injection and refrigerated storage technique, and keep all clinic appointments
pk: Erythropoietic response over days to weeks; hemoglobin rise titrated over weeks
Long terminal half-life, approximately 130-140 hours (about 6 days), enabling extended-interval dosing
Sustained effect supports every-2-week and once-monthly dosing
Refrigerate at 2-8 C (36-46 F); do not freeze; protect from light; do not shake
pearls: This is the pegylated long-acting recombinant erythropoietin Mircera (methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta) - the FDA-approved 'pegylated rHuEPO'

BOXED WARNING (ESA class): increased death, serious cardiovascular/thromboembolic events, and (in cancer) tumor progression/shortened survival - use the lowest dose to avoid transfusion and do NOT target hemoglobin above 11 g/dL in CKD
Long half-life (~6 days) allows every-2-week then once-monthly dosing - a key advantage over epoetin
NOT indicated for chemotherapy-induced anemia in cancer patients
Sudden loss of response with very low reticulocytes suggests antibody-mediated pure red cell aplasia - stop and do not switch to another ESA; ensure iron repletion and BP control for optimal effect
missed: If a scheduled (every-2-week or monthly) dose is missed, administer it as soon as possible and resume the regular dosing interval; the prescriber may adjust the schedule. Do not give extra doses to compensate, and avoid increasing the dose more often than monthly.
overdose: Overdose can produce an excessive erythropoietic response leading to hemoglobin/hematocrit elevation, hypertension, and increased thrombotic risk; very high concentrations may cause manifestations of severe polycythemia. Management includes withholding the drug and, if clinically significant polycythemia or hyperviscosity occurs, performing phlebotomy along with supportive care and blood pressure control. Monitor hemoglobin and for thrombotic complications.
